options: Put the rule in the repository's root CLAUDE.md and commit it.
Put the rule in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on the developer's machine.
Put the rule in a .claude/rules/ file with a paths: glob for test files.
Put the rule in a CLAUDE.md inside the one directory it applies to.

h.stem: The test conventions apply to every *.test.ts file, and those files are spread across 30 directories. The team wants the conventions loaded only when Claude is working on test files. Where should they go?
why: Right for conventions everyone needs in every session. This would load them for all work, not just tests.
Right for one person's preferences. Teammates wouldn't get these conventions.
A path-scoped rule loads only when Claude touches matching files, wherever they live.
Right when the files sit in one directory. These are spread across 30.

p.stem: A developer wants Claude to give terse explanations in every project they work on. Their teammates don't share the preference. Where should it go?
why: Right for team conventions. This would impose one person's preference on everyone.
User-level memory applies to all of one person's projects and isn't shared.
Right for conventions scoped to file patterns. This is a personal preference.
Right for one directory's conventions. This applies everywhere for one person.

options: Commit the conventions to the repository's root CLAUDE.md.
Split each topic into its own file and @import them from CLAUDE.md.
Run /memory to see which memory files this session has loaded.
Add a CLAUDE.md in the legacy/ directory with its own conventions.

h.stem: Claude ignores one of the team's rules in a developer's session. The developer has edited several instruction files and isn't sure which of them Claude is actually reading. What's the best first step?
why: Right when conventions live only on one person's machine. First find out what's loaded.
Right when one CLAUDE.md has become hard to maintain. This is a diagnosis problem.
See what's loaded before changing anything; the fix depends on which file is missing.
Right when one directory needs different rules. The problem here isn't known yet.

p.stem: A new teammate says Claude ignores the team's conventions on their machine; for everyone else it follows them. The conventions live in the tech lead's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. What fixes this?
why: Team conventions belong in project memory that everyone gets from the repository.
Right for organizing a large file. The conventions still wouldn't reach the teammate.
Useful for diagnosis, but the cause is already known: user-level memory isn't shared.
Right for one directory's conventions. These apply to the whole team.

options: A skill in .claude/skills/ with context: fork in its frontmatter.
A slash command in .claude/commands/, committed to the repository.
A command in ~/.claude/commands/ on the developer's machine.
A rule in CLAUDE.md so that it applies in every session.

h.stem: The team wants a /review-migration command that every developer gets automatically when they pull the repository. Where should it live?
why: Right when a skill's output would flood the session. Nothing here needs isolation.
Project commands are shared through the repository. (Today skills in .claude/skills/ work the same way.)
Right for a personal shortcut. Teammates wouldn't get it.
Right for always-on guidance. This is an on-demand command.

p.stem: A codebase-analysis skill dumps pages of exploration output into the session each time it runs, crowding out the developer's own work. What fits best?
why: Running the skill in a forked context keeps its exploration out of the main session.
Right for sharing a command with the team. The problem here is output volume.
Right for a personal shortcut. The problem here is output volume.
Right for always-on guidance. This would load more into every session.

options: Move the detailed reference material into supporting files that the skill links to.
Add argument-hint to the frontmatter so users see what to pass.
Rewrite the skill's description to say when it should be used.
Copy the skill into ~/.claude/skills/ and change the copy.

h.stem: Claude never uses the team's migration skill unprompted, even on migration tasks; people have to invoke it by name. Its description reads “Migration helper.” What fixes this?
why: Right when SKILL.md is bloated. The problem is that Claude doesn't know when to use it.
Right when users don't know what arguments to pass. It's only a hint and doesn't affect when Claude uses the skill.
Claude decides when to use a skill from its description, so the description must say when it applies.
Right for a personal variant. It doesn't help Claude recognize when to use the skill.

p.stem: A skill's SKILL.md has grown to 900 lines of reference tables. Any single run needs only a few of them, but all 900 lines load every time. What fixes this?
why: Keep SKILL.md short and load detailed material only when a run needs it.
Right when users don't know what to pass. Size is the problem here.
Right when Claude doesn't know when to use the skill. Size is the problem here.
Right for a personal variant. The copy would be just as large.

options: A skill in ~/.claude/skills/ on the developer's machine.
A skill in the repository's .claude/skills/ directory.
A section in the repository's CLAUDE.md that describes the steps.
A PostToolUse hook that runs the steps after each edit.

h.stem: A developer wants their own scaffolding workflow available in every repository they work in, without changing anything for their teammates. Where should it live?
why: User-level skills follow one person across projects and aren't shared.
Right for a team workflow. It would only exist in one repository and affect teammates.
Right for always-on conventions. This is an on-demand workflow.
Right for something that must run after every edit. This runs when asked.

p.stem: The platform team wants every engineer who works in the monorepo to get the same /new-service workflow. Where should it live?
why: Right for one person's workflow. Other engineers wouldn't get it.
A project skill is shared with everyone through the repository.
Right for always-on conventions. This is an on-demand workflow.
Right for something that must run after every edit. This runs when asked.

options: Start in plan mode and agree on an approach before any files change.
Make the change directly, then review the diff.
Have Claude interview you about the requirements before it starts.
Run the exploration in a subagent and keep only its summary.

h.stem: A developer needs to fix a typo in one error message. They know exactly which file and line it's in. What's the best way to work?
why: Right for large or ambiguous changes. Planning a one-line fix is overhead.
A small, well-understood change needs no planning step.
Right when the requirements are unclear. Here they're exact.
Right when exploration would flood the context. Nothing needs exploring here.

p.stem: The team needs to replace the logging library across 120 files. Several modules use it in unusual ways, and the team hasn't agreed on the migration pattern. What's the best way to work?
why: A large change with open design choices needs an agreed plan before edits start.
Right for a small, well-understood change. This is neither.
Right when the developer doesn't know the requirements. Here the open question is the approach.
Right when exploration would flood the context. It doesn't settle the approach.

options: Give two or three concrete input/output examples of the transformation.
Write the tests first and have Claude iterate until they pass.
Have Claude ask clarifying questions before implementing anything.
Describe all the problems in one message, because they interact.

h.stem: A developer reports bugs one at a time. Each fix breaks something another fix relied on, because all the bugs run through the same validation code. What works best?
why: Right when prose descriptions are being misread. Here the fixes conflict.
Right when behavior can be pinned down by tests. The issue here is fixing interacting bugs separately.
Right when requirements are unclear. Here the bugs are known.
Interacting problems need to be seen together, so one fix doesn't undo another.

p.stem: Claude's date parser keeps misreading what the team means by “short date.” Two rounds of prose explanation haven't helped. What works best?
why: Concrete examples remove the ambiguity that prose descriptions leave.
Right for larger behavioral specs. A few examples settle a format faster.
Right when the developer is unsure what they want. Here they know; Claude misreads it.
Right when several problems interact. Here there's one misunderstanding.

options: Write the test cases first, then have Claude iterate until they all pass.
Add the missing detail to the prompt: inputs, constraints and expected output.
Have Claude interview you about edge cases before it writes any code.
Raise the issues one per message, because they're independent.

h.stem: A developer is building a caching layer in a domain they know little about. They aren't sure which invalidation cases matter. What works best?
why: Right when the expected behavior is known. Here the developer can't write the cases yet.
Right when you know what's missing from the prompt. Here the developer doesn't know.
Questions surface edge cases the developer wouldn't think to specify.
Right for independent issues. Here the requirements aren't known yet.

p.stem: A refactored function must produce identical outputs for 40 known inputs. Claude's versions keep breaking a few of them. What works best?
why: Known expected outputs make an exact target; tests let Claude check itself.
Right when the prompt omits something. Here the target is already known.
Right when requirements are unclear. Here they're exact.
Right for independent issues. Here one target covers all of them.

options: Add a few examples of findings the team accepted and ones it rejected.
Add the team's testing and style conventions to the repository's CLAUDE.md.
Try the prompt on a sample of past PRs and refine it before rollout.
Split the prompt into separate review passes, one for each concern.

h.stem: A new review prompt is about to go live on 300 repositories. Nobody has yet seen how it behaves on real diffs. What should happen first?
why: Right when you know which judgments it gets wrong. Here nothing has been observed yet.
Right when the reviewer lacks project context. Here nobody knows how it behaves.
Refine on a sample first; problems cost far less to fix before 300 repositories depend on it.
Right when one concern crowds out others. That hasn't been observed.

p.stem: The reviewer flags “magic numbers” the team considers fine and misses the ones it cares about. A written rule describing the difference hasn't helped. What works best?
why: When a written rule fails on a judgment call, examples show where the line is.
Right when the reviewer lacks project context. Here it has a rule but misapplies it.
Right before rollout. The problem is already known here.
Right when one concern crowds out others. Here one judgment is miscalibrated.

options: Run Claude with the -p flag so that it runs non-interactively.
Use --output-format json with --json-schema for parseable output.
Include the previous run's findings so only new issues are reported.
Run the review in a separate session from the one that generated the code.

h.stem: The new CI job hangs until it times out. The logs show Claude waiting for input. What fixes this?
why: Without -p, Claude Code starts an interactive session and waits for input.
Right when downstream scripts can't parse the output. Here nothing is produced.
Right when re-runs repeat findings. Here the job never finishes.
Right when the reviewer shares the author's blind spots. Here the job never finishes.

p.stem: A script that posts inline PR comments breaks whenever Claude phrases its findings differently. What fixes this?
why: Right when the job hangs waiting for input. It runs fine here.
Schema-constrained JSON gives the script a fixed structure to read.
Right when re-runs repeat findings. Here the format varies.
Right when the reviewer shares the author's blind spots. Here the format varies.

options: Pass the prior review's findings and ask only for new or unresolved issues.
Generate the tests and review them in separate Claude sessions.
Put the project's test conventions and fixture helpers in CLAUDE.md.
Validate the JSON output against the schema and fail the job if it's invalid.

h.stem: Tests generated in CI ignore the team's fixture helpers and duplicate setup code in every file. The CI prompt doesn't mention the helpers anywhere. What fixes this?
why: Right when re-runs repeat old findings. Here the problem is missing project context.
Right when a session reviews its own work. Here the generator doesn't know the helpers exist.
CI runs read CLAUDE.md, so project conventions there reach every generated test.
Right when output breaks downstream parsing. Here the tests are valid but ignore conventions.

p.stem: Every new push gets a full set of review comments. Many repeat issues that were already raised and fixed. What fixes this?
why: With the earlier findings in context, the reviewer can report only what's new or still open.
Right when a session reviews its own output. The problem here is repetition.
Right when generated code ignores conventions. The problem here is repetition.
Right when malformed output breaks parsing. The problem here is repetition.

options: Have a separate session, without the generator's context, review the code.
Run the review overnight on a schedule instead of on every push.
Give the reviewer the PR description and linked issue as context.
Give the review job read-only tools so it can't change the branch.

h.stem: The session that generates code in CI then reviews its own output. It rarely finds problems that human reviewers later catch. What fits best?
why: A reviewer without the generator's reasoning doesn't share its blind spots.
Right when cost matters more than fast feedback. Timing isn't the issue here.
Right when the reviewer misreads intent. Here it's too close to the code it wrote.
Right when the reviewer must not modify the branch. Here it misses issues.

p.stem: The reviewer flags intentional behavior changes as bugs because it doesn't know what each PR is meant to do. What fits best?
why: Right when the reviewer shares the author's blind spots. Here it lacks the PR's intent.
Right when cost matters more than speed. It doesn't explain the change's intent.
Telling the reviewer what the change is for lets it tell intended changes from bugs.
Right when the reviewer must not modify the branch. Here it misjudges intent.
